1 Introduction
Grapevine phenology regulates the seasonal timing of growth and reproduction, shaping expo-
sure to frost, heat and water limitation as well as the scheduling of vineyard operations (Jones
and Davis, 2000; Tomasi et al., 2011). Earlier budburst can alter spring frost exposure, while
shifts in flowering, veraison and ripening change the climatic conditions experienced during
fruit development. Warming therefore affects both the suitability of wine-growing regions and
the choice of cultivars and management practices (Van Leeuwen et al., 2024). Reliable pheno-
logical predictions are essential for assessing seasonal development across contrasting growing

environments.
Process-based phenology models predict developmental stages by accumulating temperature-
dependent rates until specified requirements are reached (Chuine and Régnière, 2017). Forcing-
only models represent heat accumulation from a prescribed or calibrated date without explicitly
simulating dormancy. Examples include growing degree days (GDD) and the Grapevine Flower-
ing Veraison (GFV) model (Parker et al., 2011). Chilling–forcing models additionally represent
the cold exposure associated with dormancy release. In sequential models, forcing begins only
after a chilling requirement is fulfilled; in parallel models, chilling and forcing can accumulate
over overlapping periods, with forcing effectiveness potentially depending on chilling status
(Chuine, 2000).
Within these families, temperature-response functions provide another dimension of model com-
plexity. Forcing can increase linearly above a base temperature, approach a plateau through a
sigmoid function, or decline above an optimum through a beta function. Chilling responses
range from threshold-based accumulation to triangular and smooth nonlinear functions; triangu-
lar formulations developed for trees require evaluation for grapevine (Chuine, 2000). Fila et al.
(2014) compared linear and beta forcing-only models with beta-based chilling–forcing models,

spans.text: idence that base-temperature selection can matter more than explicit dormancy representation
(García de Cortázar-Atauri et al., 2009), these findings favour independent evaluation of model
components rather than assuming that greater complexity improves prediction.
Hybrid approaches offer a complementary route to improved prediction by combining process-
based models (PMBs) with machine learning (Reichstein et al., 2019). Residual learning retains
the process-based model prediction and estimates its systematic error from additional environ-
mental covariates. This can represent statistical associations omitted from a temperature-driven
formulation, but does not establish the underlying physiological mechanisms. Its usefulness
depends on whether the correction transfers beyond the conditions represented during calibra-
tion. Spatially dependent observations can make random record-level validation overoptimistic,
reinforcing the need for evaluation at independent sites and under contrasting environmental
conditions (Roberts et al., 2017).
Temperature representativeness adds uncertainty in complex terrain, where regional weather
stations and gridded climate fields cannot fully resolve vineyard-scale conditions. Local tem-
perature and phenological timing vary with environmental setting, making the spatial scale of
weather information relevant to prediction (Neethling et al., 2019; de Rességuier et al., 2026).
Elevation-based adjustments offer a simple means of accounting for part of this spatial mismatch,
although they cannot fully describe inversions, aspect effects or canopy microclimates. Conse-
quently, the value of increasing process-based model complexity or adding residual learning
may depend on how well the temperature input represents the growing environment.
This study examines three complementary approaches to improving grapevine phenology predic-
tion across contrasting European environments. The objectives are to (i) evaluate how process-
based model structure, including forcing and chilling functions and their sequential or parallel
interaction, affects predictive accuracy and environmental transferability; (ii) quantify the con-

tribution of DEM-based elevation correction and its variation across terrain and environmental
zones; and (iii) assess the additional contribution of residual machine learning and its depen-
dence on model structure and temperature input.

spans.text: 2 Materials and methods
2.1 Overall workflow
The factorial design crosses ten process structures, RAW or DEM-corrected temperature, and
absent or present TabM residual learning, yielding forty configurations for each of BBCH07,
BBCH65, BBCH81 and BBCH89 (Fig. 1). Phenology, weather and terrain matching (panel
a) precede the paired temperature inputs (panel b) and model combinations (panel c). All ad-
justable parameters and residual learners are fitted within calibration groups (panel d). Locked
predictions provide paired comparisons at held-out sites within the primary environmental-zone
split. Terrain analyses quantify variation in predictive correction benefits (panel e).

2.3.1 Phenology observations
Observations came from TEMPO (Maury et al., 2023), DWD (Kaspar et al., 2014) and PEP725
(Templ et al., 2018). Data were provided by the members of the PEP725 project; its extract was
accessed on 1 July 2026. One canonical representation of each source preserved provider iden-
tities and licences. Records retained source-qualified site identifiers, reported variety, country,
WGS84 coordinates, calendar date and directly recorded BBCH code. Inferred stage conver-

sions and observations before 1951 were excluded. BBCH07 and BBCH09 remained distinct
(Lorenz et al., 1995).
Exact duplicates required agreement of all seven fields. Different accepted dates or variety
labels remained separate; dates were neither aggregated nor repaired. Missing varieties and
DWD maturity classes did not imply cultivar or individual-plant identity. Source-qualified sites
can share physical locations and were grouped conservatively for validation.
Screening first applied inclusive stage-family calendar windows, then checked all observed stage
pairs within separate vegetative and reproductive branches at the same source-qualified site,
reported variety and year. Each record required at least one compatible counterpart date when
the other stage was present. Unsupported records were removed simultaneously, and checks
repeated until stable. When neither endpoint had support, both stage groups were quarantined;
missing endpoints imposed no constraint. Exact branch orders, calendar windows for the four
target stages and major-phase intervals are in Tables 2–3; windows for other observed stages are
specified in Supplementary Methods S6. These project screening choices are not physiological
limits, were not tuned against model errors and never constrain predictions. All excluded records
retain original fields and rule/date evidence.
The revised four-target screen incorporates source quality, annual-report precedence and revised
calendar and interstage bounds (Supplementary Methods S6). These revised observations supply
both process calibration and residual learning. Eligible observations retain the original weather-
complete site–years, exact numeric coordinates, country and calibration/test assignments. Rel-
ative to the earlier 74,311-record modelling cohort, 503 records are removed and 810 records
are restored, producing 74,618 observations at 3,169 reported sites and 26,443 site–years during

spans.text: 3.5 Predictive gains from residual learning
Under raw temperature forcing, residual TabM correction reduced held-out MAE in all forty
model–stage comparisons (Fig. 9a). Four-stage gains ranged from 2.87 to 6.08 d across the
ten hybrids, with all ten pointwise 95% intervals excluding zero (Fig. 9b). The fixed-model
average gain was 4.10 d (95% interval: 3.56–4.63 d). Stage-specific average gains were 3.90,
4.89, 3.38 and 4.21 d for budburst, flowering, veraison and maturity/harvest, respectively. These
comparisons used a common finite-scoring population of 15,105 observations at 633 held-out
sites in 355 independence groups.
Larger ML gains generally accompanied larger errors in the original process model. Across the
ten structures, four-stage process-model MAE ranged from 11.27 to 14.61 d, whereas hybrid
MAE occupied the much narrower range of 8.30–8.75 d. The highest-error process model, CL-
FB-P, improved from 14.61 to 8.53 d, a gain of 6.08 d; the lowest-error process model, CB-FL-S,
improved from 11.27 to 8.40 d, a gain of 2.87 d. Thus, the larger correction did not produce
the lower final error. The lowest hybrid MAE was 8.30 d for CB-FL-P-ML, whose gain was
3.49 d. Residual learning consequently narrowed differences among process structures, while
the ranking by improvement differed from the ranking by final hybrid accuracy.
ML gains varied across environmental zones (Fig. 9c). Flowering gains were 10.58 d (9.12–
11.99 d) in EZ05 and 1.44 d (0.89–1.99 d) in EZ03. These gains reduced process-model MAE
from 15.12 to 4.54 d in EZ05 and from 9.06 to 7.62 d in EZ03 (Fig. 9d), reversing their relative
error levels. Large corrections therefore did not necessarily leave large remaining errors. The
59.85 d flowering gain in EZ01 reduced an initial MAE of 72.76 d to 12.90 d but was supported
by only five groups; no other target stage was observed there. Maturity/harvest evidence in
EZ02 and EZ03 comprised only one and four groups, respectively. These sparse estimates have
no bootstrap interval, and environmental-zone summaries describe subsets of the primary site
holdout rather than independent zone-transfer tests. Signed-bias diagnostics are reported in
Supplementary Fig. S5.
Calibration hybrid scores are apparent performance after fitting on calibration-only out-of-fold
residuals. Held-out sites supplied neither process calibration targets nor neural epoch-selection
targets. Residual learning adjusted dates only where the raw process-based model supplied a
prediction. The underlying thermal attainment remained unchanged; BBCH81 and BBCH89
could still receive the common administrative scoring date after hybrid correction.

spans.text: 4 Discussion
Process formulation, temperature input and residual learning made different contributions to
grapevine phenology prediction. Controlled structural contrasts favoured linear forcing and se-
quential chilling–forcing, while elevation correction produced a modest average improvement
with substantial variation among sites. Residual learning yielded larger gains, and DEM correc-
tion added little to average hybrid accuracy. Together, these results indicate that representing
additional processes and reducing systematic prediction errors are distinct routes to improved
performance. Their relative value depends on the phenological stage and the environments rep-
resented during calibration and testing.
4.1 Predictive value of process structure
The advantages of linear forcing and sequential interaction, averaging 1.26 and 1.41 d in the
controlled comparisons, were larger than the effect of chilling-response shape (Fig. 6). Thus,
distinguishing the timing and temperature dependence of accumulation was more consequential
for these predictions than choosing between the two tested chilling curves. The comparison also
shows why a ranking of complete models provides an incomplete account of structural perfor-
mance: an advantage averaged over matched components can coexist with weak or reversed
differences at individual stages. Veraison, for example, showed little response to the sequential–
parallel contrast despite larger differences at budburst and flowering.
The favourable performance of simpler forcing agrees with the limited benefits of increasing
complexity reported by Fila et al. (2014), but does not establish a universally preferable tem-
perature response. Field warming experiments revealed nonlinear grapevine phenological re-
sponses and interactions with source–sink conditions (Sadras and Moran, 2013). More recently,

curvilinear responses (de Rességuier et al., 2026). These differences are consistent with depen-
dence on the sampled temperature range, cultivar composition and formulation. Nonlinearity in
a developmental interval is also not equivalent to the particular daily beta response tested here.
Fixed cardinal temperatures and seasonal origins constrain the interpretation of these contrasts.

4.3 Asymmetric benefits of elevation correction
The 1.06 d average reduction in process-model MAE, equivalent to 8.4%, indicates that site-to-

Local grapevine studies show that temperature and phenology can vary substantially within a

of that variation.
The direction of elevation mismatch was more informative than a simple expectation that larger

4.4 Residual learning and its overlap with temperature correction
Residual learning reduced RAW four-stage MAE by an average of 4.10 d, with positive gains
in all forty model–stage comparisons (Fig. 9). These improvements show that useful predictive
information remained after calibration of the shared thermal requirements. Process dates and re-
cent weather histories describe the simulated seasonal state, while terrain and day length provide
additional environmental context. Their joint use can accommodate systematic discrepancies
that a single set of accumulation thresholds cannot represent. The hybrid modelling perspective
of Reichstein et al. (2019) provides a rationale for this combination of process structure and
statistical flexibility. Crop-phenology applications also demonstrate benefits from integrating
process simulations with observations through machine learning, although approaches such as
the maize framework of Ou et al. (2025) differ from residual date correction.
The dependence of ML gain on the original process error is central to interpreting these improve-
ments. Residual learning compressed the four-stage MAE range across process structures from
11.27–14.61 to 8.30–8.75 d, so weaker process baselines generally offered more scope for cor-
rection. However, gain is defined as process MAE minus hybrid MAE and therefore contains
the baseline error arithmetically. This descriptive relationship does not establish that a less ac-
curate process model is intrinsically a better input to residual learning. A large gain can reflect
substantial correction of a weak baseline while leaving a hybrid less accurate than one with a
smaller gain. Comparisons of hybrid systems consequently require final error and remaining
stage-specific limitations alongside the size of the correction.

Improved phenological estimates have potential value for directing field observations and antic-
ipating seasonal vineyard operations. Their practical usefulness depends on local error, stage
and the advance notice required for a decision. Viticultural adaptation also depends on microcli-
matic opportunities and management constraints that regional climate summaries can overlook
(Mosedale et al., 2016). Here, predictions use realized weather through the process-predicted
date, so retrospective accuracy does not establish operational forecast performance. Evaluation
at fixed issue dates, using only weather information available at issuance, is necessary before
claims about timely frost protection, treatment scheduling or harvest logistics. Independent vine-
yard observations would also allow errors to be assessed against the timing tolerances of those
decisions.
4.6 Limitations and priorities for independent validation
The observation population is geographically and biologically uneven. Germany supplies nearly
three quarters of the records, while France supplies almost all maturity/harvest observations.
Equal-site weighting limits the influence of long records but does not balance countries or cre-
ate evidence for missing country–stage combinations. Reported varieties, maturity classes and
repeated dates may represent different plants or management conditions, and monitoring identi-
fiers do not guarantee independent vineyards. Shared requirements consequently summarize a
heterogeneous population. More complete cultivar and plant identities, together with consistent

Linjia Yao, Qiang Yu and Gang Zhao
S1 Observation population and provenance

The matched modelling population contains 74,618 accepted observations at 3,169 reported sites and
26,443 site–years during 1951–2025. Sites qualify through any one of BBCH07, BBCH65, BBCH81
or BBCH89; complete stage sequences are not required. The country distribution is unequal, and some
country–stage combinations contain no observations (Table S1). Country-specific model comparisons
therefore depend on stage-specific sample sizes and attained predictions, rather than on the number of
countries alone. Record length ranges from one to 72 distinct years with at least one target observation
per site; gaps between years remain explicit and do not imply continuous monitoring.
The seven original fields are the source-qualified site identifier, reported variety, country, latitude, longi-
tude, calendar date and directly recorded BBCH code. Exact seven-field duplicates are removed, while
different accepted dates or cultivar labels remain separate. Empty variety labels are retained. A record
identifier is the SHA-256 digest of the seven-string JSON array, using UTF-8 encoding, literal Unicode
characters and compact comma/colon separators. Source provenance retains every source occurrence,
including exact duplicates, and links excluded observations to the calendar or interval evidence used in
screening. Source-qualified site identifiers distinguish reporting systems; they do not establish distinct
physical vineyards, plants or cultivars.
The historical cleaned inventory contains 259,998 records across all stages. Its original weather-complete
modelling cohort contains 74,311 target observations. The revised four-target inventory contains 75,738
records after direct-BBCH, source-quality, source-precedence and revised temporal screening. Matching
to unchanged weather-eligible site–years, country and exact numeric coordinates yields 74,618 obser-
vations: 73,808 retained in common with the historical cohort, 810 restored and 503 historical records
removed. The remaining 1,120 revised observations do not satisfy the unchanged matching require-
ments. Revised observations supply both final process calibration and residual learning. This weather-
conditioned population does not represent a random sample of European vineyards.

Six function combinations pair two forcing functions with three chilling options (the main model cat-
alogue). The two forcing-only combinations and sequential and parallel variants of the four chilling–
forcing combinations give ten process-based model structures. Linear forcing (FL) accumulates thermal
time above a fixed base temperature. Beta forcing (FB) represents a nonlinear response that peaks at an
optimum temperature and declines to zero at the upper temperature limit. Beta forcing and beta chilling

ing function was developed for forest trees; its application to grapevine is an adaptation. Temperature-
response parameters are fixed from literature and shared across stages, sites and models wherever the
